summary: Discovery focused on whether QuantaHealth should run a recall-first then rerank pipeline or an integrated rerank-first approach, plus which hosting mode to pick. Key constraints: 2k QPS burst target, P99 tail latency target of ~120ms for search responses (rerank included), strict PHI-like data residency concerns, and platform team's preference for VPC-managed private control plane. Redwood proposed a Dedicated pool with model fallbacks and a 48-hour throughput benchmark. Agreed next steps around sample data, cost comparison, and benchmark plan.
topics: current architecture: recall index + external re-ranker
vector DB sharding and hybrid search
hosting choices: Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem)

transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Avery from Redwood, AE, and with me is Diego, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Maya Patel: Good, thanks. Running a bit late but all set.
[00:09] Diego Martinez: Hi Maya, Omar, Lena. Quick note on format - we'll ask a few discovery questions then walk through options and trade-offs.
[00:15] Omar Rahman: Sounds good. We're mostly interested in a decision for our search stack: whether to keep recall-first with a light reranker or move to a heavy rerank after recall. Also, where to host — we have PHI-adjacent data so VPC/private is on the table.
[00:26] Lena Gomez: And throughput. Our internal SLAs are aggressive, we have sustained ~500 QPS with 2k burst. We need P95 ~50ms and P99 ideally <120ms end-to-end.
[00:35] Avery Chen: Great — that's the crux. Quick question: what's your current recall index and re-ranker?
[00:40] Maya Patel: We use OpenSearch for dense + sparse hybrid retrieval. For re-ranking we run a small BERT-based ranker (approx 60M params) in-house. It does batch reranking but it's getting expensive at scale.
[00:51] Diego Martinez: Okay so recall-first today with an in-house reranker. Are embeddings generated at ingestion or on-the-fly?
[00:56] Omar Rahman: At ingestion. We precompute 512-d embeddings using a proprietary embedder. Index size is roughly 40M vectors, ~2.1GB after compression per shard — actually, we have multiple shards.
[01:07] Avery Chen: That's helpful. Two axes to think about: embedding dimensionality and where reranking runs. Lower dims (e.g., 256) reduce VDB footprint and improve fanout, but may cost recall quality; higher dims (1024) improve relevance but cost more compute and memory.
[01:21] Lena Gomez: We're evaluating 512 vs 768 for a balance. Also, we are interested in Redwood's Quantized embeddings suggestions — you mentioned compact embeddings?
[01:29] Diego Martinez: Yeah, Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles by workload. For a recall-first pipeline, compact embeddings plus approximate nearest neighbor reduces IOPS and network overhead for the DB. But the reranker model size and placement will dominate tail latency.
[01:40] Maya Patel: For reranking, we can't have slow tails. If we keep rerank in path, that's an extra hop. Are customers doing the rerank in-hosted vs in Dedicated GPUs?
[01:49] Avery Chen: Both. Typical patterns: Hosted API for easier setup and fast iteration — good for dev and small prod. Dedicated pools for predictable throughput and lower per-token costs at scale. Private (VPC/on-prem) if regulatory constraints require a customer-managed network. Many customers run recall in their VDB and call Redwood for a small high-quality reranker hosted on Dedicated GPUs, sometimes colocated in the same region for minimal network latency.
[02:07] Omar Rahman: Latency is our big worry. If reranking is in the cloud and our recall is in our VPC OpenSearch, adding egress and cross-VPC hops could add 30-60ms. Any ways to mitigate?
[02:16] Diego Martinez: Yes — Redwood supports private endpoints and VPC peering options for Dedicated and Private deployments. With Private (customer-managed control plane) you can keep traffic within your VPC and use our inference nodes in the same subnet. That removes public egress and keeps latency down. There's also a hybrid hosting: you can keep recall on your VDB and run rerank on a Dedicated Redwood pool inside your cloud account (we've done this with AWS PrivateLink and VPC endpoints).
[02:35] Maya Patel: Costs — Dedicated looks pricey but predictable. How do we think about per-query econ if we push a 175M reranker vs a 1.3B reranker?
[02:44] Avery Chen: Good question. Rough heuristics: smaller rerankers reduce latency and cost per query; larger models improve MRR/precision. Redwood Optimize can simulate expected token counts and suggest batching and KV cache policies. Also, fallbacks are common: route high-confidence queries to a smaller reranker and only call the large model for edge cases or low-confidence scores. That reduces unit cost significantly.
[02:59] Lena Gomez: What's the tradeoff of doing rerank-first (i.e., run a small ranker over a broader candidate set early) vs recall-first?
[03:06] Diego Martinez: There's nuance. Recall-first keeps retrieval efficient and relies on the reranker to reorder top candidates. Rerank-first (or cascade) can prune earlier with a cheap ranker applied to a larger candidate set to improve quality downstream — this saves on heavy reranker calls but increases initial compute and can complicate latency curves. For high QPS, recall-first with a cascade rerank works well: compact ANN for recall, then a mid-sized ranker, then occasional large model.
[03:28] Omar Rahman: Ok, we like cascade attempts if it reduces calls to big models. But we also need clear SLOs and fallbacks when the big model is slow or unavailable. How does Redwood handle graceful degradation?
[03:38] Avery Chen: Redwood has smart routing and automatic fallback to smaller model variants or regional fallbacks. For Dedicated, you can define canary rollouts and A/B and set automatic fallback policies to a compatible model when latency or capacity thresholds are hit. Also caching of reranker outputs for repeated queries helps reduce calls.
[03:51] Maya Patel: About vector DB — we're on OpenSearch but exploring moving to a specialized VDB like Pinecone. If we switch, how does Redwood integrate?
[03:59] Diego Martinez: Redwood integrates with major VDBs via standard protocols (ANN query over gRPC/HTTP). We also provide connectors and best-practice configs for sharding/fanout. Important things: ensure shard fanout doesn't blow up QPS and watch for cold-start IO. Redwood Optimize will flag shard sizes and suggest embedding dims that match your index layout.
[04:16] Lena Gomez: Can you expand on sharding and fanout? We have 6 shards across regions and current fanout for a query is all shards — that drives latency.
[04:23] Diego Martinez: Right — full fanout increases recall but also increases latency. Strategies: route queries to subset shards using routing keys, prefiltering, or use a two-level index (category-level recall then shard-level). We also recommend topology-aware query routing and edge caching for very hot records. For some customers, a hybrid approach with a lightweight initial filter (sparse + compact embed) reduces fanout by 60% and keeps recall acceptable.
[04:42] Omar Rahman: Security checklist: we need SOC2 Type II, SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, KMS support, and ideally an option for on-prem. Do you have those?
[04:52] Avery Chen: Yes. Redwood provides SOC2 attestations, SSO via SAML/OIDC, RBAC in the Console, audit logs (configurable retention), and KMS/HSM integrations for Private deployments. On-prem is available as a Private deployment package for regulated customers. We'll share the whitepaper and SOC2 report.
[05:05] Maya Patel: Great. For the benchmark, what does Redwood need from us?
[05:09] Diego Martinez: Sample corpus (2GB preferred), representative query log (with QPS profile and peak patterns), and target SLOs. We'll run a 48-hour throughput benchmark against both Hosted and Dedicated configs: measure median, P95/P99, token/unit costs, and failure modes. We'll also test fallback behavior under load.
[05:24] Lena Gomez: Re: embeddings dimensionality — if we move to 256 dims and quantize, how big a drop in recall should we expect?
[05:31] Diego Martinez: It depends on your data. For many corpora, going from 512->256 with a good quantization profile yields minor recall degradation (1-3% recall lift loss) but huge savings in storage and throughput. But for fine-grained medical semantics, sometimes 512 or 768 is safer. We recommend running an offline eval with your query set to measure the exact impact — Redwood can help run those evals.
[05:49] Omar Rahman: Do you support sparse + dense hybrid queries (we sometimes run keyword boosting and dense similarity simultaneously)?
[05:55] Avery Chen: Yes — Redwood's routing supports hybrid search patterns. You can run a weighted combination of sparse + dense signals and then rerank the merged candidate list. We have customers that use BM25 prefilter + ANN recall + tiny reranker to get high precision with lower cost.
[06:06] Maya Patel: One operational question — we're concerned about model drift and quality regressions after updates. How do you monitor quality?
[06:12] Diego Martinez: Redwood Optimize provides eval hooks: tie quality monitoring to prompt/query sets, surface regression alerts, and integrate with your CI for model rollouts. For rerankers, we track ranking metrics over time, alert on drops, and can automate rollbacks.
[06:24] Lena Gomez: For SLA — can Dedicated guarantee tail latency?
[06:28] Avery Chen: Dedicated gives predictable throughput and is SLA-backed for uptime and baseline latency targets, but exact P99 guarantees depend on workload and model choices. We supply expected performance profiles for model variants — if you need hard P99 guarantees we can scope a performance SLA in the contract with runbook and performance testing clauses.
[06:43] Omar Rahman: Let's go back to costs. If we run a cascade: compact recall (Host local) -> mid-size rerank on Dedicated -> large model fallback, what ballpark savings should we expect vs calling large reranker for all queries?
[06:55] Diego Martinez: It varies, but customers often see 4-6x reduction in per-query cost on average because the large model is invoked only on 10-20% of queries. Also infra costs drop because the heavy model needs fewer instances to handle the same effective load. We'll put numbers in the cost comparison sheet tailored to your QPS and hit patterns.
[07:14] Maya Patel: How do you instrument cost breakdowns? We need token-level and call-level granularity for showbacks.
[07:19] Avery Chen: Redwood Console shows token-level cost, per-route and per-model breakdowns, and you can export reports. For Dedicated, we also provide reserved capacity accounting and per-customer allocation.
[07:28] Lena Gomez: One more tech detail — what about KV cache across requests for multi-turn rerank? Can we share KV cache among requests to speed up?
[07:34] Diego Martinez: We support KV cache policies that persist across requests for the same session and cache warmed prefixes. For rerank pipelines, we often cache intermediate embeddings and partial reranker outputs for a short TTL to avoid repeated work for similar queries. Cache semantics are configurable in Dedicated and Private deployments.
[07:48] Maya Patel: Ok, let's talk timeline. We want a pilot in Q2. What should the PoC look like?
[07:53] Avery Chen: Typical PoC: 4-week pilot — first week: data handoff and environment setup (VPC endpoints if needed), second: baseline metrics and offline evals, third: run the live 48-hour throughput benchmark and iterate on model/dim choices, fourth: analyze and give recommendations plus contract terms for Dedicated or Private.
[08:09] Omar Rahman: If we do Private (on-prem), what's involved? We have air-gapped options.
[08:13] Diego Martinez: Private on-prem requires a bit more engineering: appliance deployment, connectivity for optional telemetry, and we integrate with your KMS/HSM. It gives you full control over networking and data residency but increases time-to-deploy (typically 6-12 weeks depending on infra). We'll provide an on-prem runbook.
[08:27] Maya Patel: Any customers with similar regulated data doing Dedicated + VPC?
[08:31] Avery Chen: Yes — several healthcare and finance customers run Dedicated in their cloud accounts with VPC peering/private endpoints; a few run Private on-prem for higher assurance. We'll share anonymized case studies.
[08:40] Lena Gomez: Errors and fallback testing — what happens during model OOM or node failures?
[08:44] Diego Martinez: Redwood runtime has automatic fallback routing, cross-region failover, and can route to a smaller, compatible model on capacity issues. We also do graceful degradation where we return last-known-good ranking if needed. For Dedicated, redundancy and autoscaling policies help mitigate OOM.
[08:59] Maya Patel: If we sign up for a Dedicated pool, can we pin a model version for reproducibility?
[09:04] Avery Chen: Absolutely. You can pin model versions and control rollouts. Redwood Console supports canary deploys and rollbacks.
[09:10] Omar Rahman: From an ops perspective, what's the onboarding support? We need SRE-level runbooks.
[09:15] Diego Martinez: Dedicated and Private customers get an onboarding SE, a solutions packet with runbooks, and access to our observability integrations. We also provide tracing hooks and per-route dashboards.
[09:26] Maya Patel: Great. So recapping — you will send the cost comparison, benchmark plan, security docs, and we will send sample data. Anything else?
[09:33] Avery Chen: We'll also propose a recommended pilot architecture (cascade pattern + Dedicated reranker in VPC), and a config for the benchmark that mirrors your traffic shape.
[09:40] Lena Gomez: One last question: managing model drift — can Redwood run periodic offline evals and alert us?
[09:46] Diego Martinez: Yes, Redwood Optimize can schedule evaluators and send regression alerts; we can integrate with PagerDuty or Slack.
[09:52] Maya Patel: Perfect. Thanks everyone. Let's lock in next week for the technical deep-dive — Thursday works for us.
[09:58] Avery Chen: We'll propose times in the follow-up email. Thanks all.
[10:02] END
